title: Intracranial hypotension secondary to spinal arachnoid cyst rupture presenting with acute severe headache: a case report
case_prompt: A 51-year-old Indian woman presented with a sudden-onset, severe bilateral occipital headache that began three days earlier without prodrome or visual aura. The continuous pain was exacerbated by coughing, relieved when recumbent, and radiated over the vertex to the temporal regions; it was also associated with nausea and mild photophobia. She had no prior headaches, no significant medical history, and no regular medications. There was no family history of headache or sudden death. On examination, she was alert with normal vital signs. The neurologic examination was unremarkable: Kernig’s sign was negative, there was no neck stiffness or rash, and fundoscopy showed no papilledema. Initial labs showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia; erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were normal. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture revealed no red cells, an opening pressure of 11 cm H2O, and no xanthochromia. A magnetic resonance angiogram of the head was normal. With symptomatic improvement on bed rest and weak opioid analgesia, she was given a tentative diagnosis of migraine and discharged.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Subarachnoid hemorrhage was considered then excluded — “Her history of acute-onset severe headache suggested a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) brain scan proved normal. A lumbar puncture showed no evidence of red cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the opening pressure was normal at 11 cm/H2O. Spectrophotometric examination of the CSF was negative for xanthochromia.”  
2. Bacterial meningitis was considered then excluded — “Neurological examination was normal and Kernig's sign was negative. There was no neck stiffness and no rash. Initial investigations revealed a mild leucocytosis with a neutrophilia but inflammatory markers were normal (erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/hour; C-reactive protein level <5 mg/L).”  
3. Intracranial aneurysm was considered then excluded — “A magnetic resonance angiogram was performed to exclude the presence of an intracranial aneurysm. This was normal.”  
4. Migraine was diagnosed but is less likely given orthostatic worsening and poor response to simple analgesia — “In light of the negative investigations and symptomatic improvement with bed rest and weak opioid analgesia, a tentative diagnosis of migraine was made.”  
5. Spontaneous intracranial hypotension best explains the orthostatic headache and persistent symptoms, supported by later MRI findings — “A repeat magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan revealed new bilateral thin (<1 cm) subdural collections suggesting the possibility of reduced intracranial pressure. An MRI of the spinal cord demonstrated a large right-sided spinal arachnoid cyst at the level of T10/11 … The pleural effusion on the right suggests cyst rupture.”
